before:
Hamlet is the story of a Danish prince who is told by his father's ghost that his uncle murdered him to take the throne — and is asked to avenge it. Hamlet spends most of the play not avenging it. He pretends to be mad, stages a play to confirm the ghost's claim, hesitates over a clear opportunity, accidentally kills the wrong man, drives the woman he loves to suicide, gets shipped to England, comes back, and kills his uncle only after his uncle's poison has already killed him.

It is the longest of Shakespeare's plays — about 4,000 lines — and the one with the most language about language. Hamlet talks more than any other character in any other Shakespeare play. The famous soliloquies — "To be or not to be," "O what a rogue and peasant slave am I," "How all occasions do inform against me" — are not interruptions of the action; they are the action. Hamlet is a man trying to decide whether to act, and the play is mostly the inside of that deciding.

Written around 1600, Hamlet sits at a hinge in Western literature. It inherits the conventions of revenge tragedy — the ghost, the play-within-a-play, the bloody final scene — and uses them to do something none of its predecessors had done: to put a recognizably modern interior life on stage. Hamlet doubts. He performs. He watches himself perform. He cannot tell whether his own grief is genuine or theatrical. The play does not resolve those questions. It is most haunting at the moments when its hero is most uncertain about what he is doing and why.
after:
At Elsinore, the guards are watching for a ghost. Hamlet, son of the dead king, mourns his father and is disturbed by his mother’s marriage to the king’s brother, Claudius. When the ghost describes a murder and demands revenge, Hamlet must judge both the message and its messenger. Can he trust a spirit? What would count as proof? And who will be harmed when he acts?

This is more than the story of a man who delays. Hamlet investigates, performs, mocks, threatens, and acts suddenly as well as reflectively. Others watch him and try to direct him. Conversations become traps, affectionate advice can lead to surveillance, and a performance becomes an attempt to uncover a crime. Horatio, Ophelia, Laertes, and Gertrude each have a place in a conflict Hamlet cannot control alone.

Read it as a play: notice who is present, who listens unseen, and who speaks only to the audience. Public speech, private thought, songs, and the players’ speeches sound different. The text is arranged in five acts and twenty scenes.

before.title: Mad or performing madness?
before.text: Hamlet tells Horatio he will put on an "antic disposition." But by Act IV it is less clear who is in control. Notice when his behaviour serves a strategic purpose — and when it seems to have slipped the leash.
before.angleObjective: I want to read Hamlet as a study in madness — whether his is real or performed, and what the difference tells us about sanity itself.

before.title: The problem of acting under uncertainty.
before.text: Everyone else in the play — Claudius, Laertes, Fortinbras — acts decisively. Hamlet thinks. The play takes his thinking seriously rather than dismissing it. Ask what he actually knows, and when.
before.angleObjective: I want to understand why Hamlet cannot act — what stops him when every other character in the play seems to know exactly what to do.

before.title: Revenge vs. justice.
before.text: The ghost demands Hamlet kill Claudius. But Hamlet wants more than death — he wants punishment that fits the crime, guilt that is witnessed. That distinction drives every delay in the play.
before.angleObjective: I want to read this as a meditation on revenge versus justice — why revenge feels demanded but keeps being deferred.

before.title: Thinking too much.
before.text: "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all." Hamlet says it himself. But the play is not sure it agrees. Watch whether his reflectiveness is a flaw or a form of moral seriousness that the world he lives in cannot accommodate.
before.angleObjective: I want to trace the relationship between overthinking and paralysis — whether Hamlet's intelligence is his greatest asset or the thing that destroys him.

after.title: Who knows what?
after.text: The ghost’s story, the king’s reactions, and the conversations behind tapestries provide different kinds of evidence. Distinguish what you see as a reader from what any one character can know.
after.angleObjective: I want to follow how suspicion becomes conviction and what evidence people use to justify their decisions.

after.title: Playing a part
after.text: Hamlet announces an intention to act mad. That does not make every feeling a performance or every action part of a plan. Compare his conversations with his friends, his soliloquies, and his treatment of Ophelia.
after.angleObjective: I want to examine performance, grief, and loss of control without deciding their boundaries in advance.

after.title: The consequences of revenge
after.text: Hamlet, Laertes, and Fortinbras are each connected with a father’s legacy. Their responses differ. Watch who demands revenge, who tries to direct it, and who pays its costs.
after.angleObjective: I want to compare revenge with responsibility and see how one action changes other people’s choices.

after.title: Words doing several jobs
after.text: A pun may flirt, insult, evade, or threaten. Images of disease, acting, ears, and poison recur. Listen for changes in register, especially when a character borrows or mocks another person’s language.
after.angleObjective: I want to hear the different voices and track the images people use to understand and influence one another.

before.name: Hamlet
before.description: Son of the murdered king, nephew of the new king, once intimate with Ophelia, friend of Horatio. He returns from university at Wittenberg to find his father dead, his mother remarried to his uncle, and his world collapsed. He is brilliant, witty, contemptuous, grieving, and paralyzed. The play is the inside of his mind — and he is the most fully imagined human being in the English canon.

before.name: Claudius
before.description: Hamlet's uncle, the new king. He has murdered his brother, married his brother's widow, and taken his brother's throne. He is a competent ruler and a guilty man. The scene in which he tries to pray and finds he cannot — because he is unwilling to give up what the murder bought him — is one of the most theologically precise moments in Shakespeare. Not a cartoon villain. A man who chose.

before.name: Gertrude
before.description: Hamlet's mother, widow of the murdered king, now married to his murderer. The play does not reveal whether she knew. Hamlet rages at her in the closet scene; she does not deny what he says, and she does not confirm it. She loves her son. She drinks the poisoned cup at the end — Shakespeare leaves it ambiguous whether by accident or as a choice — and her death is the one Hamlet shows real grief for.

before.name: Ophelia
before.description: Daughter of Polonius, sister of Laertes, briefly the woman Hamlet loved. Her father uses her as bait to spy on Hamlet, and Hamlet — already half-mad, already cruel — destroys her in the "get thee to a nunnery" scene. After her father is killed by Hamlet, she goes mad herself, sings broken songs, and drowns in a stream. Her madness is the play's quietest tragedy, the one nobody notices in time.

before.name: Polonius
before.description: Lord Chamberlain, father of Ophelia and Laertes. A garrulous old courtier who dispenses sententious advice ("to thine own self be true") and meddles in everyone's business. Hamlet kills him by accident, stabbing through a curtain in his mother's bedroom, mistaking him for the king. His death is the moment after which the play moves from the tragedy of the mind to the tragedy of consequence — a chain of corpses follows.

before.name: Horatio
before.description: A scholar and Hamlet's only true confidant. He survives the play. Hamlet trusts him absolutely — "a man that fortune's buffets and rewards / Hath ta'en with equal thanks." At the end, with Hamlet dying in his arms, Horatio is the one who will live to tell the story. The play's last instruction, almost — "absent thee from felicity awhile" — is Hamlet asking Horatio not to follow him into death so the truth can be reported.

after.name: Hamlet
after.description: Son of the dead king and Gertrude. A student at Wittenberg, he wants to understand what happened to his father. Wit and reflection coexist with grief, cruelty, and impulsive action.

after.name: Claudius
after.description: The old king’s brother and Gertrude’s new husband. Labelled KING in the dialogue, he seeks to protect both the kingdom and his own position as Hamlet’s behavior arouses suspicion.

after.name: Gertrude
after.description: Hamlet’s mother and Claudius’s wife, bound to both her son and her new husband. What she knows at each point should be inferred from her words and reactions rather than assumed in advance.

after.name: The Ghost
after.description: Appears in the form of the old King Hamlet and calls for revenge. Its account of murder and the afterlife begins the action, but Hamlet also questions what kind of spirit he has encountered.

after.name: Ophelia
after.description: Has received Hamlet’s declarations of love. Her father and brother warn her against him, and the court’s investigation of the prince intrudes on their relationship. Her later songs connect love, loss, and mourning.

after.name: Polonius
after.description: Father of Ophelia and Laertes. He gives elaborate advice and gathers information through questions and hidden observation. What happens onstage often tests his confident explanations.

after.name: Laertes
after.description: Ophelia’s brother, who travels to France and later returns. His family loyalties and demand for redress offer an important comparison with Hamlet’s.

after.name: Horatio
after.description: A scholar who sees the ghost and becomes Hamlet’s confidant. He helps observe, remember, and eventually recount what has happened.

after.name: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern
after.description: Summoned by the king and queen to keep Hamlet company and discover the cause of his change. Friendship and service to the court come to pull in different directions.

after.name: Fortinbras
after.description: Nephew of Norway’s present king and son of the Fortinbras defeated by the old King Hamlet. His military plans give the Danish court’s conflict an external setting.

after.name: The players, gravediggers, and Osric
after.description: The players display the force of emotion and performance. The gravediggers joke about death, rank, and law. The courtier Osric’s elaborate speech immediately invites Hamlet’s mockery.

before.title: The Birth of the Modern Self
before.body: Harold Bloom argued that Shakespeare invented the human as it is now understood, and Hamlet is exhibit A. Before Hamlet, characters in literature were largely consistent — Achilles is angry, Odysseus is cunning, Antigone is devoted. Hamlet contradicts himself. He doubts himself. He is one thing in soliloquy, another with Ophelia, a third with Horatio, a fourth with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. He watches himself feel grief and wonders whether the feeling is real. That self-watching, self-doubting, self-correcting consciousness is what an inner life now means — and it begins, in literature, with this play. Almost every sustained interior monologue since (in the novel as much as in drama) is in some way working downstream of what Shakespeare did with Hamlet's mind. The first modern character is a man who cannot decide whether to act.

before.title: Doubt as a Way of Being
before.body: The play's central problem is not Claudius — the king is fairly easily damned by the play-within-a-play — but Hamlet's own incapacity. He has the proof. He has the opportunity. He still does not act. The play refuses to give a single explanation for that hesitation. Hamlet himself proposes several — cowardice, depression, religious scruple, philosophical caution, theatrical relish — and dismisses each. Modern readers from Coleridge to Goethe to Freud have proposed others, and the play absorbs them all. That refusal of a single answer is what keeps the play alive. Doubt is not depicted here as a flaw to be cured but as a condition to be inhabited. Hamlet matters now because his predicament — being given a clear duty and finding it impossible to discharge cleanly — is one modern readers recognize as their own. The play is the canonical literary text for the problem of acting under uncertainty.

before.title: Language That Will Not Settle
before.body: Hamlet is the play in which Shakespeare's language is most aware of itself. Hamlet puns relentlessly. He plays words against words, meanings against meanings, registers against registers. Polonius speaks in clichés and the play exposes them as clichés. Claudius speaks in court rhetoric and Hamlet hears the rhetoric. The play is full of moments where a single word — "seems," "fashion," "word" itself — opens up and refuses to close again. This linguistic restlessness is part of why Hamlet is endlessly quotable: "to thine own self be true," "there are more things in heaven and earth," "the lady doth protest too much," "method in his madness," "the rest is silence." Read in sequence, those quotations form a pocket-anthology of what English literature has done with language since. To read Hamlet is to read English at the moment it became fully capable of saying anything.

after.title: Thought changing as we hear it
after.body: Hamlet’s soliloquies do not simply announce finished opinions. They test possibilities, accuse him, and change direction. His later actions have no simple relationship to those thoughts. The play makes this movement visible without giving one explanation that fits every choice.

after.title: A court of watchers
after.body: People watch one another, hide, interpret letters, and turn others into experiments. The play-within-the-play concentrates that pattern: a staged action is meant to reveal something, but its audience does not necessarily understand it in the same way. Readers also judge signs whose meaning the characters dispute.

after.title: Grief and power beyond the prince
after.body: The royal family’s conflict harms people around it. Ophelia and Laertes show that Hamlet’s grief is not the play’s only grief. Questions of monarchy, popular support, and war continue alongside it. Personal and political consequences remain closely connected.
